items.prompt: Which AWS service provides resizable virtual servers that you can launch in the cloud?

options.label: Amazon EC2
Amazon S3
Amazon RDS
Amazon VPC

rubric: EC2 provides virtual servers called instances.
S3 is object storage, RDS is managed databases, VPC is networking; learners confuse these with compute.

items.prompt: What type of storage is Amazon S3?

options.label: In-memory cache
Object storage
Relational database
Block storage

rubric: S3 stores data as objects in buckets.
Block storage describes EBS, a common confusion.

items.prompt: What does IAM stand for in AWS?

options.label: Instance and Application Manager
Integrated Account Metrics
Internal Access Monitor
Identity and Access Management

rubric: IAM is Identity and Access Management, used to control who can do what.
Other options are plausible-sounding invented expansions.

items.prompt: Which AWS service is a managed relational database service supporting engines such as MySQL and PostgreSQL?

options.label: Amazon DynamoDB
Amazon S3
Amazon RDS
Amazon Route 53

rubric: RDS is the managed relational database service.
DynamoDB is a NoSQL key-value service, often confused with RDS.

items.prompt: What is an AWS Region?

options.label: A single data center building that hosts all of an account's resources
A family of EC2 instance types tuned for one workload
A group of linked billing accounts that share one invoice
A separate geographic area containing multiple Availability Zones

rubric: A Region is a geographic area with multiple AZs.
Learners often equate a Region or AZ with a single data center.

items.prompt: Which of the following are AWS database services? Select all that apply.

options.label: Amazon Aurora
Amazon CloudFront
Amazon DynamoDB
Amazon EBS

rubric: DynamoDB and Aurora are database services.
CloudFront is a CDN and EBS is block storage.

items.prompt: A new team member must create a private network section in AWS where their servers will run, with their own IP address range and subnets. Which AWS service is used to define this virtual network?

options.label: AWS Lambda
Amazon VPC
Amazon SNS
Amazon CloudWatch

rubric: VPC lets you define an isolated virtual network with subnets.
CloudWatch is monitoring; Lambda is serverless compute; SNS is messaging.

items.prompt: Why would you store a website's images in S3 instead of on an EC2 instance's local disk?

options.label: S3 storage is free of charge for any amount of data
S3 keeps data durably and independent of any one server
S3 objects can be edited in place faster, like blocks on a local disk
S3 is required because an EC2 instance cannot store files locally at all

rubric: S3 offers durable storage separate from instance lifecycle.
Distractors assume S3 behaves like a disk, is mandatory, or is free.

items.prompt: What does it mean that an IAM policy follows the principle of least privilege?

options.label: Permissions expire automatically after a set time, such as one day
Users start with full access and lose permissions they don't use
Only the root user may hold any permissions in the account
Users get only the permissions needed for their tasks

rubric: Least privilege grants the minimum permissions required.
Other options misread it as default-open, root-only or time-limited.

items.prompt: Why do architects deploy an application across two Availability Zones?

options.label: So data is stored in two countries automatically
So it keeps running if one zone has a failure
So the bill is cut in half by sharing
So it runs twice as fast on every request

rubric: Multiple AZs provide fault tolerance.
Learners mistake AZs for performance, country distribution or cost savings.

items.prompt: What is the main difference between a public subnet and a private subnet in a VPC?

options.label: A public subnet routes to an internet gateway; a private one does not
A public subnet is billed per hour; a private subnet has no hourly charge
A public subnet holds only databases; a private one holds only servers
A public subnet sits in a different Region from the private subnet

rubric: Public subnets route to an internet gateway.
Distractors invent cost, region or role differences.

items.prompt: Which statement best explains how EC2 pricing with On-Demand instances works?

options.label: You pay a fixed yearly fee for each instance, whether or not it runs
You pay for the compute time you use, with no long-term commitment
You pay an upfront fee once and then own the physical server outright
You pay a reduced rate only while the instance is stopped and idle

rubric: On-Demand is pay-as-you-go.
Distractors describe reservations, inverted billing or ownership.

items.prompt: Which statements correctly describe IAM roles? Select all that apply.

options.label: They let an EC2 instance access S3 without stored access keys
They are the same thing as the root account
They provide temporary credentials to a service or user that assumes them
They must be tied to one person's password

rubric: Roles give temporary credentials, avoiding hard-coded keys.
Roles are not passwords or the root account.

items.prompt: A developer stores an access key in a file on an EC2 instance so the app can read an S3 bucket. A colleague suggests attaching an IAM role to the instance instead. Why is the role the better choice?

options.label: It makes the S3 bucket public to the instance, so the app no longer needs any credentials
It supplies temporary credentials automatically, so no long-lived key sits on the disk
It encrypts the instance's disk and the key file on it, so a stolen key cannot be used
It gives the app the same rights as the root user, so S3 requests are never denied

rubric: Roles avoid storing long-lived secrets.
Distractors misstate roles as making buckets public, encrypting disks, or granting root.

items.prompt: Which description best matches Amazon S3?

options.label: Block storage that attaches to one EC2 instance as a disk
Object storage that holds files as objects in buckets, found by key
A virtual firewall that filters traffic for individual instances
A managed relational database that runs SQL queries for apps

rubric: S3 is object storage: data is stored as objects in buckets and addressed by key.
Block storage describes EBS, and the firewall option describes security groups.

items.prompt: A security group allows inbound HTTP (port 80) to a web server, and users receive pages back. Why do the responses get out without an extra rule?

options.label: Security groups are stateful, so replies to allowed requests are permitted
Security groups are stateless, so replies are matched by default rules
HTTP is exempt from filtering, so responses bypass all group checks
Network ACLs sit on the instance and mirror inbound rules outward

rubric: Security groups are stateful: return traffic for an allowed connection is automatically allowed.
Statelessness is a property of network ACLs, which learners often confuse with security groups.

items.prompt: Why is it better for an application on EC2 to use an IAM role than access keys saved in a config file?

options.label: A role is exempt from permission policy checks, so the app can call any service it needs
A role gives the instance one set of keys that stay valid until an admin rotates them
The role supplies temporary credentials automatically, so no long-term keys sit on disk
Saved access keys are rejected by S3 for instance traffic, while a role is accepted there

rubric: Roles deliver short-lived credentials to the instance, avoiding stored long-term secrets.
Roles still need policies, and access keys do work with S3.

items.prompt: What is an Availability Zone in AWS?

options.label: One or more data centers in a Region, with independent power
A pricing tier that sets the discount for long-running instances
A private network range that you define inside your own account
A geographic area that contains exactly one data center building

rubric: An AZ is one or more discrete data centers within a Region with separate power and networking.
A Region contains multiple AZs, so the single-building option confuses the two.

items.prompt: Compared with installing a database yourself on an EC2 instance, what does Amazon RDS take over for you?

options.label: Choosing which indexes and data types give the best app results
Routine work like OS patching, automated backups and failover
Deciding which users in your company should be allowed to read data
Designing the schema and writing the queries your app needs

rubric: RDS manages operational tasks like patching, backups and failover configuration.
Schema design, indexing and access decisions remain the customer's responsibility.

items.prompt: Which statements correctly describe Amazon EBS volumes? Select all that apply.

options.label: A volume is automatically copied to every Region you use
A volume is attached to an instance in the same Availability Zone
A volume can keep its data after the attached instance is stopped
A volume is accessed over HTTP as objects inside a bucket

rubric: EBS volumes persist independently of instance state and must be in the same AZ as the instance.
Object access over HTTP describes S3, and EBS does not replicate across Regions automatically.

items.prompt: A developer opens a VPC and sees two subnets. The route table of subnet A has a route sending 0.0.0.0/0 to an internet gateway. The route table of subnet B has only the local VPC route. What can the developer conclude?

options.label: Both are public, because every subnet in a VPC can reach the internet by default once an internet gateway is attached to the VPC
Neither is public until an Elastic IP is attached to the subnet itself, since public addressing is configured per subnet, not per route
A is public and B is private, because B has no internet route
A is private and B is public, because B has fewer routes and so fewer paths that could block inbound internet traffic

rubric: A subnet is public when its route table sends internet traffic to an internet gateway.
Having fewer routes does not make a subnet public, and Elastic IPs attach to instances, not subnets.

items.prompt: You must upload `report.csv` from your current directory to the folder `reports/` in the bucket `my-bucket`. Which command does this?

options.label: `aws s3 mb report.csv s3://my-bucket/reports/`
`aws s3 cp report.csv s3://my-bucket/reports/`
`aws ec2 cp report.csv my-bucket:reports/`
`aws s3 cp s3://my-bucket/reports/ report.csv`

rubric: `aws s3 cp <local> <s3-uri>` copies a local file to S3.
The reversed form downloads, `mb` makes a bucket, and `ec2` has no cp for this.

items.prompt: You need SSH access to an EC2 instance only from your office, whose public IP is 203.0.113.10. Which inbound security group rule fits?

options.label: TCP port 22, source 0.0.0.0/0
TCP port 22, source 203.0.113.0/8
TCP port 22, source 203.0.113.10/32

rubric: SSH uses TCP 22, and /32 limits the source to exactly one address.
0.0.0.0/0 opens SSH to everyone, 3389 is RDP, and /8 allows a huge range.

items.prompt: A VPC uses 10.0.0.0/16 and already has a subnet 10.0.1.0/24. Which new subnet CIDR fits inside the VPC without overlapping that subnet?
rubric: 10.0.2.0/24 lies within 10.0.0.0/16 and does not share addresses with 10.0.1.0/24.
10.0.1.128/25 is inside the existing subnet, and the other two ranges are outside the VPC.

items.prompt: Which IAM policy statement gives read-only access to the objects in the bucket `logs-prod`?

options.label: Allow `s3:*` on `arn:aws:s3:::logs-prod/*`
Allow `s3:GetObject` on `arn:aws:s3:::logs-prod/*`
Allow `s3:PutObject` on `arn:aws:s3:::logs-prod/*`
Allow `s3:GetObject` on `arn:aws:s3:::logs-prod`

rubric: GetObject on the objects ARN (bucket/*) grants read-only access to the objects.
s3:* grants more than read, the bucket ARN alone does not match objects, and PutObject writes.

items.prompt: Running `ssh -i mykey.pem ec2-user@203.0.113.25` fails with 'UNPROTECTED PRIVATE KEY FILE! Permissions are too open.' What should you run next?

options.label: `chmod 400 mykey.pem`
`chown ec2-user mykey.pem`
`rm mykey.pem`
`chmod 777 mykey.pem`

rubric: SSH requires the private key file to be readable only by its owner, so `chmod 400` fixes it.
`chmod 777` makes it more open, and chown or deleting the file does not fix the permissions.

items.prompt: You must make a web app survive the loss of one Availability Zone. Which two actions help achieve this? Select all that apply.

options.label: Run instances in two AZs behind an Application Load Balancer
Use an Auto Scaling group spanning two AZs with a minimum of 2 instances
Attach an Elastic IP to one instance and keep it running
Move everything to one larger instance in a single AZ

rubric: Spreading instances across AZs with a load balancer and Auto Scaling keeps the app up if one AZ fails.
A single bigger instance or one Elastic IP remains a single point of failure.

items.prompt: An EC2 instance sits in a private subnet and must download OS updates from the internet, yet nothing from the internet may start a connection to it. The VPC already has an internet gateway and a public subnet. What should you add?

options.label: An inbound security group rule allowing all traffic from 0.0.0.0/0 on the instance
A NAT gateway in the public subnet, with a private route to it for 0.0.0.0/0
An egress-only internet gateway attached to the VPC, with a route to it for 0.0.0.0/0
A route from the private subnet straight to the internet gateway for 0.0.0.0/0

rubric: A NAT gateway in a public subnet gives outbound-only internet access to private instances via a route.
Routing straight to the internet gateway makes the subnet public, and opening inbound rules adds exposure.

items.prompt: A web server in a public subnet must serve HTTPS to the whole internet, but SSH must work only from the office range `203.0.113.0/24`. Which inbound security group rules do this?

options.label: TCP 443 and TCP 22 both from `203.0.113.0/24`

rubric: Open 443 to the world and restrict 22 to the office CIDR.
Other options swap the sources or open SSH to everyone, missing which port needs which scope.

items.prompt: Versioning is enabled on an S3 bucket. You run `aws s3 rm s3://logs-bkt/app.log` without a version ID. What happens?

options.label: The request fails until versioning is suspended
A delete marker is added and earlier versions remain
All versions of the object are permanently deleted
The latest version is deleted and the older one is promoted

rubric: A plain delete on a versioned bucket adds a delete marker; old versions stay recoverable.
Distractors assume deletion is permanent or blocked.

items.prompt: An application on an EC2 instance must read objects from one S3 bucket without storing any long-term credentials on the instance. What should you do?

options.label: Store an IAM user's access keys in an encrypted file on the instance's EBS volume
Attach an IAM role with S3 read permission via an instance profile
Make the bucket public and restrict access with a bucket policy on the VPC's IP range
Pass an IAM user's access keys to the instance as user data at launch time

rubric: Instance profiles supply temporary credentials automatically.
Stored keys or public buckets violate the no-long-term-credentials requirement.

items.prompt: Instances in a private subnet need outbound internet access to download patches, but must not accept inbound connections from the internet. Which route table entry achieves this?

options.label: `0.0.0.0/0` to a NAT gateway in a public subnet
`0.0.0.0/0` to an internet gateway
`0.0.0.0/0` to a virtual private gateway
`10.0.0.0/16` to a NAT gateway in the private subnet

rubric: A NAT gateway in a public subnet gives outbound-only access.
Routing directly to an internet gateway makes the subnet public.

items.prompt: You want to upload the local folder `./site` to `s3://my-bucket/site`, copying only new or changed files on repeat runs. Which command fits?

options.label: `aws s3 sync ./site s3://my-bucket/site`
`aws s3 cp ./site s3://my-bucket/site`
`aws s3 mv ./site s3://my-bucket/site`
`aws s3 ls ./site s3://my-bucket/site`

rubric: `sync` compares and copies only differences recursively.
`cp` without `--recursive` fails on folders and `mv` deletes the source.

items.prompt: You must make a web tier behind an Application Load Balancer tolerate the loss of one Availability Zone. Which actions do this? Select all that apply.

options.label: Move all instances to one larger instance type in a single AZ
Enable the ALB in subnets from at least two AZs
Launch instances in subnets in at least two AZs
Attach an Elastic IP to each instance in the same AZ for failover

items.prompt: An Auto Scaling group has 4 instances and a target tracking policy of 50% average CPU. Traffic rises and average CPU reaches 75%. Max size is 10. Roughly what will the group do?

options.label: Scale out to the maximum of 10 instances right away
Scale out to about 6 instances to bring CPU near 50%
Wait until CPU passes 90% before adding any instances
Add one instance per cycle, as simple scaling does

rubric: Target tracking scales proportionally: 4 x 75/50 = 6.
The other options assume a jump to the maximum, a high threshold delay, or fixed one-instance steps, ignoring proportional scaling.

items.prompt: An EC2 instance in a new subnet has a public IP and a security group allowing SSH, yet connections time out. The VPC has an internet gateway. Which cause is most likely?

options.label: The internet gateway must be attached to the instance's network interface, not only to the VPC
The security group needs an outbound rule allowing port 22, because replies are not tracked
The subnet's route table lacks a `0.0.0.0/0` route to the internet gateway
The instance needs an IAM role that grants permission to accept SSH sessions

rubric: A subnet is public only if its route table sends internet traffic to the IGW.
Security groups are stateful so replies need no outbound rule; IAM doesn't govern network SSH.

items.prompt: A Lambda function in private subnets of a VPC times out when calling DynamoDB, but works when not attached to a VPC. The subnets have no NAT gateway. What is the best diagnosis?

options.label: The execution role lacks dynamodb:GetItem permission, so calls hang
The function has no network path to DynamoDB's public endpoint
The security group blocks inbound responses from DynamoDB
DynamoDB tables must sit in the same subnet as the function

rubric: VPC-attached Lambda needs a NAT or a gateway VPC endpoint to reach DynamoDB.
Missing IAM permission yields an AccessDenied error, not a timeout.

items.prompt: A user's IAM policy allows `s3:*` on a bucket. The bucket policy has an explicit Deny for requests not coming from a specific VPC endpoint. The user calls from a laptop. What is the result?

options.label: Denied, because an explicit deny overrides any allow
Allowed, because the identity policy grants `s3:*`
Denied, because bucket policies always override identity policies
Allowed, because the user is in the same account

rubric: An explicit deny always wins in policy evaluation.
The last option overstates it: bucket policies only win here because of the explicit deny.

items.prompt: A team moves 2 TB of objects read daily into S3 Standard-IA to save money, and the bill rises. What best explains this?

options.label: Standard-IA bills each GET request at a higher rate, and request fees outweigh any storage savings
Standard-IA charges per-GB retrieval fees that outweigh storage savings for frequent reads
Standard-IA replicates objects across multiple Regions, so storage is billed once per Region copy
Standard-IA has a higher per-GB storage rate than Standard, so every stored object costs more

rubric: IA lowers storage price but adds retrieval fees, which suit infrequently accessed data.
Other options invent pricing behaviors.

items.prompt: A reporting-heavy application slows down because many read queries hit the primary RDS instance. The database already uses Multi-AZ. Why won't Multi-AZ help, and what would?

options.label: Multi-AZ only helps writes; enable Provisioned IOPS only
Multi-AZ standby is not readable; add a read replica
Multi-AZ replicates asynchronously; switch to a single AZ
Multi-AZ standby is readable but needs a larger instance type

rubric: Standard Multi-AZ standby exists for failover and does not serve reads; read replicas scale reads.
Others confuse availability with read scaling.

items.prompt: An ALB shows all targets as unhealthy though the application runs on the instances. Which could be causes? Select all that apply.

options.label: The health check path returns HTTP 404
The instances lack a public IP address
The app listens on a port different from the health check port
The instance security group doesn't allow traffic from the ALB

rubric: Blocked traffic, bad path, or wrong port each fail health checks.
A public IP isn't needed as the ALB reaches targets via private IPs.

items.prompt: Account A owns bucket `data-a` whose bucket policy allows account B's root principal `s3:GetObject`. A role in account B with no S3 permissions in its policies gets AccessDenied reading objects. What is the cause?

options.label: The bucket policy only works for public access, so the bucket's Block Public Access must be disabled first
The role also needs an identity policy in account B allowing S3 access
Bucket policies can grant access to users in other accounts but not to roles, which need trust policies
The role must be recreated in account A, since a bucket can only trust roles from its own account

rubric: Cross-account access requires an allow on both the resource side and the caller's identity side.
Others misstate how cross-account trust works.

items.prompt: An EC2 instance in a subnet with no public IP cannot reach package repositories. The subnet's route table has `0.0.0.0/0` pointing directly at an internet gateway. What is the most likely cause?

options.label: The route table needs a more specific route for each repository address, because an internet gateway ignores a default route and only forwards traffic matching explicit destination prefixes
The internet gateway cannot route outbound traffic, so the subnet needs a virtual private gateway attached to the VPC before instances can reach public sites
The security group is stateful and blocks the return traffic, so an inbound rule allowing the repository addresses must be added before replies can reach the instance
The internet gateway only translates addresses for instances with a public or Elastic IP, so private-only instances need a NAT gateway

rubric: An internet gateway performs one-to-one NAT only for instances with public IPs, so private-only instances need a NAT gateway.
Distractors misread stateful security groups and the role of virtual private gateways.

items.prompt: A role has `s3:GetObject` on a bucket and the bucket policy allows it, yet reads of SSE-KMS encrypted objects fail with AccessDenied. Other unencrypted objects in the bucket read fine. What is the most likely cause?

options.label: The bucket policy must also name the role's account number in a separate statement for encrypted objects to be readable
S3 blocks all SSE-KMS reads unless the request comes from the same region through a gateway VPC endpoint
The role lacks `kms:Decrypt` permission via the key policy or a grant, so the object cannot be decrypted
The objects' storage class prevents decryption until they are restored by an explicit lifecycle transition

rubric: Reading SSE-KMS objects needs permission to use the KMS key in addition to S3 permissions.
Distractors invent S3-side restrictions rather than checking the KMS layer.

items.prompt: A web server's security group allows inbound 443. The subnet's network ACL has inbound allow 443 and outbound allow 443 only, with default deny otherwise. Clients time out. Why?

options.label: The server needs an Elastic IP, since responses on ephemeral ports are dropped by the internet gateway
The network ACL is stateful, so it blocks the connection until the inbound rule is replicated outbound
The security group is stateless, so it needs an explicit outbound rule to answer the client requests
The network ACL is stateless, so the outbound rule must allow the ephemeral ports used by client responses

rubric: Network ACLs are stateless, so return traffic to the client's ephemeral port needs an outbound allow.
Distractors swap the stateful/stateless behaviour of security groups and network ACLs.

items.prompt: A Lambda function attached to private subnets in a VPC times out when calling DynamoDB, but worked before it was attached to the VPC. The subnets have no NAT gateway. What is the best diagnosis?

options.label: DynamoDB tables only accept connections from the internet, so the function must be moved back to public subnets
The subnets have no path to DynamoDB, so a gateway VPC endpoint or NAT route is needed
Lambda functions in a VPC lose IAM permissions, so the execution role must be recreated with DynamoDB access
The function's memory is too low once attached to a VPC, so the network interface fails to initialise

rubric: Attaching to a VPC removes default internet access; DynamoDB needs a gateway endpoint or NAT path.
Distractors blame IAM, DynamoDB exposure or memory instead of routing.

items.prompt: A team enabled RDS Multi-AZ (standard instance deployment) expecting read-heavy dashboards to speed up, but read latency on the primary is unchanged. What explains this?

options.label: Replication to the standby is synchronous, which adds latency on every read and cancels any gain
The standby exists for failover only and does not serve reads, so read scaling needs read replicas
Multi-AZ only protects storage, so the compute size of the primary must be raised to improve reads
The standby serves reads only after a failover test has been run, which has not yet happened

rubric: The standby in a Multi-AZ instance deployment is for availability and does not serve reads.
Distractors confuse availability with read scaling.

items.prompt: A user's identity policy allows `s3:*` on a bucket, yet `PutObject` returns AccessDenied in the same account. Which could explain this? Select all that apply.

options.label: The bucket is in a different region than the user's console session
A service control policy in the organization that denies S3 writes
A permissions boundary on the user that does not include `s3:PutObject`
An explicit Deny in the bucket policy that matches the user's request
The bucket policy has no Allow for the user, so the identity policy alone is ignored

rubric: Permissions boundaries, explicit denies and SCPs all cap or override identity allows.
Group-attached policies still apply, and console region does not affect S3 authorisation.

items.prompt: An Auto Scaling group behind an ALB keeps terminating new instances a minute after launch and replacing them in a loop. The app needs about five minutes to start. The ELB health check is used with a health check grace period of 60 seconds. What is the root cause?

options.label: The launch template's AMI is corrupted, so each instance fails its EC2 status checks after boot
The grace period ends before the app is ready, so failed ELB health checks mark instances unhealthy
The scaling policy's cooldown is too short, which forces the group to add instances faster than it needs
The ALB deregistration delay is too long, which causes instances to be removed before they have started

rubric: Health checks start counting after the grace period; with a 60s grace and 5 minute startup, instances are replaced prematurely.
Distractors blame deregistration, AMI or cooldown, which don't produce this pattern.

items.prompt: Application logs in S3 have unpredictable access: some months nothing is read, others many objects are. The team wants no retrieval fees, no manual lifecycle tuning and low storage cost. Which storage choice best fits?

options.label: S3 Intelligent-Tiering, because it moves objects between tiers automatically with no retrieval fees
S3 One Zone-IA for all objects, because it is cheapest and is designed for unpredictable access
S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval, because it has the lowest storage price and retrieval is typically fast
S3 Standard-IA for all objects, because it has lower storage cost and no retrieval charge

rubric: Intelligent-Tiering adapts to unpredictable access without retrieval charges.
Distractors ignore IA retrieval fees or the retrieval delay in Glacier.

items.prompt: A production database server runs 24/7 at steady load and must never be interrupted. The commitment is acceptable for three years. Judged on cost and reliability, which purchasing option is best?

options.label: A Compute or EC2 Instance Savings Plan, because it discounts steady usage without interruption risk
Spot Instances, because they are the cheapest and the workload can be restarted from backup
Dedicated Hosts on-demand, because they guarantee no interruptions and are cheaper than any commitment
On-Demand Instances, because they cost less than commitments when usage is steady and predictable

rubric: Savings Plans or reservations give a large discount for steady usage with no interruption risk.
Spot can be interrupted; On-Demand costs more for steady loads.

items.prompt: A CI job in account A must deploy to account B. Criteria: no long-lived secrets, auditable per-session activity, and revocable centrally. Which approach best meets them?

options.label: Create a role in account B trusting account A's job role, and have the job call `sts:AssumeRole`
Create an IAM user in account B and store its access keys in the CI system's secret store
Create a shared admin IAM user in both accounts and rotate its password every ninety days
Make the deployment bucket public in account B and let the job push artifacts without credentials

rubric: Cross-account roles issue temporary credentials, logged per session, and are revoked by editing the trust or policy.
Distractors rely on long-lived keys, shared users or public access.

items.prompt: A web app needs path-based routing to several services, TLS termination and integration with AWS WAF. Traffic is HTTP/HTTPS only. Which load balancer best meets these criteria?

options.label: Classic Load Balancer, because its single listener can route requests by URL path and attach AWS WAF web ACLs
Gateway Load Balancer, because it inspects HTTP paths and terminates TLS for backend services
Application Load Balancer, because it routes on HTTP paths and integrates with AWS WAF
Network Load Balancer, because it operates at layer 4 and supports WAF rules on listener ports

rubric: ALB works at layer 7 with path rules, TLS termination and WAF integration.
NLB and GWLB don't offer path-based routing or WAF.

items.prompt: A service needs an RTO of 15 minutes and an RPO of seconds after a regional outage, and the team cannot rely on launching and configuring new compute during the outage. Budget rules out full active-active. Which disaster recovery strategy best fits?

options.label: Pilot light with only the database replicated, because compute can be launched from images after the failover
Backup and restore, because snapshots copied cross-region are cheapest and can be restored after failover
Cold standby with infrastructure code stored, because it has zero running cost and deploys after failover
Warm standby with a scaled-down running stack and continuous replication, scaled up on failover

rubric: Warm standby with continuous replication meets a seconds-level RPO and 15-minute RTO below active-active cost.
Backup/restore and cold options typically exceed the RTO; pilot light is slower to scale.

items.prompt: A proposal stores a database password in plain text in EC2 launch template user data. Which are valid criticisms? Select all that apply.

options.label: User data is always encrypted at rest with the instance's KMS key, so exposure is impossible
User data is limited in size, so a password cannot fit
Anyone with permission to describe the launch template can read the password
The password is retrievable from the instance metadata service by any process on the instance
The password cannot be rotated without creating a new launch template version

rubric: User data is readable via API and instance metadata and is hard to rotate, so Secrets Manager or Parameter Store is better.
User data is not automatically encrypted for readers, and size limits don't block a password.

items.prompt: A production VPC spans three AZs. A team proposes one NAT gateway in a single AZ to save about two-thirds of NAT cost. Criteria: the app must keep outbound access to external APIs during a single-AZ failure, and cost matters but is secondary. What is the best judgement?

options.label: Use one NAT instance on a small EC2 size, because it is cheaper and survives AZ failure by default
Use one NAT gateway per AZ with matching route tables, because it avoids a cross-AZ dependency
Keep one NAT gateway, because it automatically fails over to another AZ when its own AZ fails
Replace NAT with an internet gateway on private subnets, because it removes the single point of failure

rubric: A NAT gateway is AZ-scoped; one per AZ keeps outbound access when an AZ fails, satisfying the primary criterion.
Distractors assume automatic cross-AZ failover or misuse IGWs and NAT instances.

items.prompt: A teammate says a role in account A can read objects in an S3 bucket in account B once the role's identity policy allows s3:GetObject on that bucket's ARN. Which critique is correct?

options.label: Wrong: the identity policy alone is enough, because the role is already authenticated inside AWS and the bucket owner has no say
Wrong: cross-account reads need an S3 ACL on every object, because bucket and identity policies cannot grant across accounts
Wrong: the bucket policy in account B must also allow the role, because cross-account access needs an allow on both sides
Wrong: only the bucket policy matters, so the role needs no S3 permissions in account A because the bucket owner decides

rubric: Cross-account access requires an allow in the caller's identity policy and in the resource policy of the other account.
Distractors assume one side suffices or that only ACLs work across accounts.

items.prompt: Private-subnet workers pull about 40 TB a month from S3 in the same Region through a NAT gateway. Criteria: cut cost, keep traffic off the public internet, make no code changes. Which option is best?

options.label: Add an S3 gateway endpoint and route-table entry, removing NAT data-processing charges for that S3 traffic
Add a second NAT gateway in each AZ, since spreading the traffic lowers the per-GB processing charge
Replace NAT with an S3 interface endpoint, since gateway endpoints are billed per GB in the same way as NAT
Move workers to public subnets with Elastic IPs, since that avoids NAT charges and still stays private

rubric: S3 gateway endpoints have no hourly or per-GB charge and keep traffic on the AWS network.
Distractors misread NAT pricing, or use public subnets, which sends traffic through the internet gateway.

items.prompt: In a design review someone says: 'An RDS read replica in another AZ gives us automatic failover with zero data loss, so we can skip Multi-AZ.' Which evaluation is right?

options.label: Wrong: replication is asynchronous and promotion is manual, so Multi-AZ is needed for zero-loss failover
Right: replicas replicate synchronously, and RDS promotes them automatically whenever the primary instance fails
Right: replicas share the primary's storage volume, so no committed writes can be lost when failing over
Wrong: replicas must sit in the primary's AZ and so give no protection against an AZ outage or failure

rubric: Read replicas are asynchronous and need manual promotion; a Multi-AZ standby is synchronous with automatic failover.
Distractors confuse replicas with Multi-AZ standbys or invent shared storage.

items.prompt: Steady compute of about $20 per hour runs 24/7 for the next year. During the year the team will move some services from EC2 to Fargate and change instance families. Criterion: maximise discount while keeping that flexibility. Which is best?

options.label: Standard Reserved Instances for the current instance family, since they give the deepest EC2 discount but tie the commitment to that family
A one-year Compute Savings Plan, since the hourly commitment applies across EC2, Fargate and Lambda usage
On-Demand pricing with no commitment, since it keeps full flexibility to change services but gives no discount on the steady baseline
Spot Instances for the baseline, since they give the largest discount but can be interrupted when AWS reclaims capacity

rubric: Compute Savings Plans discount usage across instance families and services such as Fargate.
Standard RIs lock the instance family; Spot suits interruptible work, not a steady baseline.

items.prompt: Objects of several MB have unpredictable access patterns. Requirements: millisecond retrieval, no retrieval fees, and lowest storage cost without manual analysis. Which S3 storage class is best?

options.label: S3 Intelligent-Tiering, since it moves objects between access tiers automatically without retrieval fees
S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval, since archive classes always give the lowest cost per GB stored
S3 One Zone-IA, since using one zone is cheaper and retrieval fees do not apply to that class
S3 Standard-IA, since its infrequent-access pricing is lower and retrieval stays immediate

rubric: Intelligent-Tiering adapts to unpredictable access with no retrieval charges and millisecond access.
Standard-IA and One Zone-IA charge retrieval fees; Glacier Flexible Retrieval is not millisecond.

items.prompt: A design runs an Auto Scaling group across two AZs in private subnets, with one NAT gateway in AZ-a, IAM user AdministratorAccess keys stored in a file on each instance, and RDS Multi-AZ. Which criticisms are valid? Select all that apply.

options.label: The single NAT gateway makes AZ-a a dependency for outbound traffic from instances in both AZs
Instances in private subnets cannot receive patches, so they should be moved into public subnets
RDS Multi-AZ is redundant because the Auto Scaling group already protects the database tier from failure
The keys are long-lived and over-privileged; an instance role with least-privilege permissions would be safer

rubric: Static admin keys violate least privilege and role-based credentials; one NAT is an AZ-level single point of failure.
Auto Scaling does not protect stateful databases, and private instances can be patched via NAT or endpoints.

items.prompt: A nightly job runs about 5 hours, is CPU-heavy, and writes checkpoints to S3 every 5 minutes so it can resume after interruption. Finance wants the lowest cost, and the job has a 10-hour window. Which compute choice best fits?

options.label: An always-on On-Demand EC2 fleet sized for peak load, since long jobs need uninterrupted capacity to finish reliably
AWS Batch on EC2 Spot capacity, resuming after interruptions, since the window allows retries
Lambda functions chained by Step Functions, since Lambda removes idle cost and each step can run in parallel
Fargate On-Demand tasks, since they avoid instance management and cost less than Spot for long jobs

rubric: Checkpointed, deadline-tolerant work suits Spot, which is the cheapest capacity.
Distractors ignore the 15-minute Lambda limit, pay for idle fleets, or assume On-Demand beats Spot.

items.prompt: CloudTrail logs from all accounts must be tamper-resistant even against administrators of the source accounts, and retained for 7 years. Which design meets this?

options.label: An organization trail to a log-archive bucket with a lifecycle rule moving objects to Glacier after one day
Trails in each account writing to CloudWatch Logs with 7-year retention and access limited to administrators
An account trail to a bucket in the same account, with versioning and MFA delete enabled for 7 years
An organization trail to a bucket in a separate log-archive account with Object Lock in compliance mode for 7 years

rubric: A separate account plus Object Lock compliance mode prevents deletion or alteration even by privileged users.
Same-account, lifecycle-only or log-group designs can still be changed by administrators.

items.prompt: A Lambda function in a VPC must reach an RDS MySQL database. Requirements: no database password in code or environment variables, and surviving bursts of 1,000 concurrent invocations without exhausting connections. Which design meets both?

options.label: Run Lambda outside the VPC and use a public RDS endpoint with a password stored in Parameter Store
Connect directly with a KMS-encrypted password in an environment variable and a raised max_connections setting
Connect through RDS Proxy using IAM database authentication, with the Lambda role allowed rds-db:connect
Connect directly, reading the password from Secrets Manager on each invocation and opening a new connection

rubric: RDS Proxy pools connections and IAM authentication removes the stored password from the function.
Other options keep passwords in the function path or leave connection exhaustion unsolved.

items.prompt: A game needs players in us-east-1 and eu-west-1 to write locally with low latency, tolerate a full Region loss, and see replication lag of about a second. Which data layer meets all of these?

options.label: RDS Multi-AZ in us-east-1 with a cross-Region read replica in eu-west-1 promoted manually on failure
Aurora Global Database with the writer in us-east-1 and a read-only secondary cluster in eu-west-1
DynamoDB with AWS Backup copying snapshots to eu-west-1 hourly and restoring after a Region loss
DynamoDB global tables with replicas in both Regions, and clients using their local Region's endpoint

rubric: Global tables give multi-Region active-active writes with replication typically within about a second.
Aurora Global has a single writer; backup copies and replicas give far worse RPO and no local writes.

items.prompt: A vendor's AWS account must read only the `exports/` prefix of your bucket. Requirements: no long-lived keys, and protection against the vendor's other customers tricking the vendor into using your role. Which design meets this?

options.label: A role trusting any principal, protected only by a unique ExternalId and a policy limited to the prefix
A role trusting the vendor's account with a unique ExternalId condition and permissions limited to the prefix
An IAM user for the vendor with access keys scoped to the prefix, rotated every 90 days
A public-read bucket policy on the prefix, with an unguessable object-key naming scheme to deter outsiders

rubric: A role trusted by the vendor account with ExternalId avoids long-lived keys and mitigates the confused deputy problem.
Other options use static keys, trust anyone, or rely on obscurity.

items.prompt: Instances in private subnets with no internet route must use SQS and S3, and only principals from your AWS Organization may use these paths. Which design meets this?

options.label: An internet gateway and public IPs on the instances, with IAM policies restricting the queue and the bucket
An interface endpoint for SQS and a gateway endpoint for S3, with endpoint policies on aws:PrincipalOrgID
A NAT gateway with security groups that allow only the published AWS public IP ranges for SQS and S3
Gateway endpoints for both SQS and S3, with a network ACL limiting traffic to the organization's accounts

rubric: SQS uses an interface endpoint and S3 a gateway endpoint; endpoint policies can restrict by organization ID.
SQS has no gateway endpoint, NACLs cannot filter by account, and NAT or public IPs break the no-internet requirement.

items.prompt: You must serve a static site worldwide at https://www.example.com from a private S3 bucket. Which components belong in a design that meets this? Select all that apply.

options.label: An ACM certificate requested in us-east-1 and attached to the distribution
The bucket made public with a website endpoint, so CloudFront can fetch objects without extra policies
An ACM certificate requested in the bucket's Region, since CloudFront reads certificates from the origin's Region
A Route 53 alias record for www pointing to the distribution
A CloudFront distribution using origin access control, with a bucket policy allowing only that distribution

rubric: OAC keeps the bucket private, CloudFront certificates must be in us-east-1, and an alias record maps the domain.
Public buckets break the private requirement, and the origin Region is irrelevant for CloudFront certificates.

items.prompt: An order pipeline sends messages to an SQS standard queue consumed by Lambda. Malformed messages are retried until the 4-day retention expires, then vanish unseen, while using up consumer capacity. Requirements: no message silently lost, and poison messages set aside for inspection. What is the design missing?

options.label: A switch to a FIFO queue, since FIFO queues automatically discard messages that cannot be processed
A visibility timeout of zero, so that failed messages return at once and are retried much faster
A dead-letter queue with a redrive policy and maxReceiveCount, plus an alarm on its depth
A longer retention period of 14 days, so that failing messages have more time to eventually succeed

rubric: A DLQ isolates messages after repeated failures so they can be inspected rather than expiring silently.
Longer retention, FIFO, or zero visibility timeout do not isolate poison messages and may worsen the problem.
